places.name: Cúc Viên Thôn
places.size: A small harbour village of about 35 houses and 150 people, half hidden by banked chrysanthemum beds across about 15 hectares.
places.where: Grassland at sea level on a flat coast. Earth qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the hot spring Hoàng Cúc Thang 90 km, the village Tân Sinh 226 km. Villagers hid Phượng Minh's scouts in the flowers in 586. Map crop: a small bowl-valley of paddy plots and a braided stream between rolling golden-brown hills with forest pockets, opening north-east to a blue bay; the village sits at the valley's seaward end.
places.imagined: Autumn: gardens grown so thick that the paths between cannot be seen.
places.subject: The place: Cúc Viên Thôn, Chrysanthemum Garden Village, seen from above a small harbour on a flat coast in autumn. Setting: a small bowl-valley of green and gold paddy plots and a braided stream between rolling golden-brown hills, opening to a little round harbour of calm blue-green water on a bay to the north-east, a low breakwater of stones, and the sea beyond. About thirty-five grey-tile roofs are half hidden by banked beds of yellow and bronze chrysanthemums that fill every slope and yard, in tiers and terraces, thick as a quilt about fifteen hectares across, in gold, bronze, rust and pale yellow, so that the village looks like roofs floating in flowers. Autumn has made the gardens so thick that the paths between them cannot be seen, only a few narrow gaps, and in one corner a bed has grown thick enough to hide a grown person, a dense tall hedge of flowers. In the harbour lie about fifteen fishing boats; nets dry on poles; a small flower market at the quay has baskets of blooms ready for the autumn rites, with a cart waiting. Villagers cut flowers into baskets, tiny figures, children running between the beds. Warm gold light from the upper left, long shadows, scent in the air. The beds are banked in tiers of dark earth, each tier held by a wall of beach cobbles, and the flowers are of eleven kinds: pale yellow, gold, bronze, rust, a rare white and a dark red. Narrow runs of stone steps cut through the terraces, mostly buried. A drying loft over the quay holds flowers hung head-down in rows for the autumn rites, and cart-loads of baskets leave for the palace each week. In the thickest bed at the village's edge a gardener stands up to his chest in blooms, and a child crouches wholly hidden.

places.name: Tang Âm Thôn
places.size: A harbour village of about 40 houses and 180 people around a caravan yard about 100 m across, shaded by one vast old mulberry.
places.where: Grassland at sea level on the coast road. Earth qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the town Tang Điền 150 km, the lava vent Chúc Dung Khẩu 152 km. Resting place of the silk caravans since 600. Map crop: a headland on the west side of a blue gulf, with the huge dark grey-brown flank of a volcanic cone rising immediately to the east and forest on its lower slopes, golden-green grass to the south and north.
places.imagined: Midday heat: carts and pack animals in the shade of the one great mulberry.
places.subject: The place: Tang Âm Thôn, Mulberry Shade Village, seen from above a coast road. Setting: a dusty coast road crossing pale-brown grassland beside a blue gulf, with a small harbour of a few boats at one side and, immediately to the east, the huge dark grey-brown flank of a volcanic cone with forest on its lower slopes. The heart of the village is a single vast old mulberry tree, about thirty metres tall, its crown spread wide, a hundred metres across, over a dusty caravan yard; the crown is a great dark-green dome. In its cool shade stand carts, pack animals (camels, mules, oxen) in lines, about thirty carts piled with bales of silk, drivers lying under the wagons, nobody tying an animal to the trunk, a bare ring left around it. The village houses, about forty grey-tile buildings, face inward toward the tree in a ring: caravan inns with long verandas and stables, fodder yards with haystacks, tea stalls, a well, farriers, and wheelwrights. A road runs in and out in both directions. A few hundred figures, tiny, drivers, innkeepers, children, tend the animals. Heat shimmers on the road beyond the shade. Bright light from the upper left, hard shadows pooling dark under the tree. The mulberry's trunk is eleven paces round, hollow on one side, and its great limbs are propped with forty timber crutches. A stone ring about three paces wide surrounds the trunk and nobody leads an animal into it. The caravan inns number nine, each with a long stable of stalls and a courtyard of hay, and a notice-board of caravan marks is nailed to a post. Water is hauled from a deep well by an ox-turned wheel, and a farrier's smithy is busy with eight pack mules. Dust glows in the shafts of light.

places.name: Hồ Tâm Thôn
places.size: A village of about 35 houses and 150 people on a small island about 200 m across in a round lake about 3 km wide, joined to the shore by a causeway.
places.where: Grassland at sea level on the coast, behind dunes. Water qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the beast lair Cự Giải Chử 195 km, the minor seat Chức Hà Các 301 km. A lake that rises and falls with the tide though it touches no sea. Map crop: a hilly grass coast of a long headland, sea to the west and a bay to the east edge, forest patch in the north-east; the lake behind the dunes is too small to show at map scale.
places.imagined: Evening, the lake breathing with the unseen sea, the notched pillar showing the water mark.
places.subject: The place: Hồ Tâm Thôn, Lake Heart Village, seen from above a coast. Setting: behind a line of pale coastal dunes lies a round lake about three kilometres across, cut off from the sea, still and mirror-blue, with a ring of reeds and a pale shore; beyond the dunes the open sea is a darker blue strip. In the middle of the lake lies a small island about two hundred metres across on which the village sits: about thirty-five grey-tile houses in a tight ring with yards, fish drying racks, small boats on the shore, a well, and a shrine. A stone causeway about six hundred metres long runs from the island to the shore. In the shallows beside the island stands a tall stone pillar notched with water marks, by which villagers read the lake's strange tide, with a rope-and-bucket stand beside it and fish traps set in lines nearby. Their sea boats, about twelve, are being djagged on rollers over the dunes to the beach by crews of villagers, tiny figures in a line. A wet band on the lakeshore shows the water has just fallen. Soft golden evening light from the upper left, long shadows. The causeway is paved with white flags and has twelve low arches for the water's rising, and the lake's rim shows pale bands of earlier water-marks all round. The pillar is notched every hand-span, with a dozen names carved at the notches where past floods stood. Fish traps are woven baskets set in the shallows in rows, a hundred of them, and a long wooden jetty runs into the lake at the village's east side. The boat rollers are logs laid at intervals in a trench across the dune, and the crews pull on ropes together.

places.name: Lô Châu Thôn
places.size: A reed village of about 45 stilt houses and 200 people on a low island in reed marsh about 1 km across, with neat harvest bays.
places.where: Grassland at 20 m on a river, reed marsh. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the forest Thủy Tùng Lâm 75 km. Carried off by Thôn Hải's raiders in 765, rebuilt in 782 reed by reed. Map crop: a river through a lowland corridor on a headland, with bare grey rocky mountains and a dark volcanic cone to the south-west, forest to the east, and the sea north of the headland's tip with a small island to the north-west.
places.imagined: A feast: the reed cutters given the first seat, reed bundles hanging above every door.
places.subject: The place: Lô Châu Thôn, Reed Isle Village, seen from above a river marsh. Setting: a river branching into channels through a wide marsh of reeds on a headland, pale gold-green in a wind, open water gleaming between, forest to the east, bare grey rocky mountains with a dark volcanic cone rising to the south-west, the blue sea beyond the headland's north tip, a hazy sky. The village stands on a low island, about forty-five houses raised on stilts with walls of bundled reeds lashed tight and grey-tile roofs, set along curving lanes of reed-mat paths that float on the water between them, with small punts moored at every house. Around the island the marsh is cut into neat bays where reed is harvested: dozens of rectangular and curved clearings, fresh-cut stubble gold-yellow, others dense and green, with cut reed stacked in tall golden stooks and bundles on rafts. Above every door hangs a bundle of reed from the rebuilding, and in a central open space the villagers hold a feast on a raised platform with long tables, the reed cutters seated first, a crowd of about two hundred, tiny figures, with lanterns and drums. Smoke from kitchens. Warm gold light from the upper left, long shadows. The reed bundles over every door are tied with a red cord and number sixty-three, one for each house the villagers rebuilt. The reed-mat paths are laid in sections two paces wide, and a dozen small bridges cross the channels. Punts carry loads of cut reed, and rafts of bound reed, a hundred paces long, wait for the weavers. A great reed hall in the middle holds the feast, with tables laid out in long lines and a platform of piled reed for the cutters. Drums are beaten in a slow rhythm, and a light haze of cooking smoke hangs in the bay.

places.name: Đan Thạch Khoáng
places.size: A quarry cut into a red mountain: a terraced face about 1.2 km wide and 300 m high, with about 30 buildings and 400 quarrymen.
places.where: High mountain at 580 m, inland. Metal qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Resource: dark-yellow stone (huyền hoàng thạch). Nearest: the ruin Tạc Thạch Trấn 75 km, the peak Thải Phượng Phong 168 km. Red stone from the phoenix's cinnabar land; cut for Xích Thành's walls from 280. Map crop: a rocky mountain mass of grey and rust-red crags with a dark volcanic cone just to the west, a blue bay of the sea at the foot to the south, dark forest and golden grass to the east and north-east.
places.imagined: Evening: raw vermilion terraces holding the day's heat, blocks waiting to be djagged down.
places.subject: The place: Đan Thạch Khoáng, the Cinnabar Stone Quarry, seen from above a red mountain. Setting: a mountain of vermilion rock in a range of grey crags that holds a dark volcanic cone just to the west, a blue bay of the sea at its foot to the south, dark forest and golden grass to the east, a haze in the valley, and a cart road snaking down toward the shore. A quarry is cut into its face in tall terraces of raw red rock, about twelve steps each some twenty-five metres high, the whole face about one kilometre and a quarter wide and three hundred metres high, glowing orange-red in the low sun, with clean square cuts and chisel marks. On the quarry floor lie rough-cut red blocks in rows, hundreds of them, each the size of a cart, waiting to be djagged down the road on log rollers by teams of oxen, with sledges, rope hoists and timber cranes on the terraces. About thirty buildings of dark timber and red tile: stone-cutters' sheds, tool forges, a long barracks, a store, and a small shrine to the stone. About four hundred quarrymen, tiny figures, cut and haul; at the end of the day some lay out sleeping mats against the warm blocks. Gold light from the upper left, deep red-violet shadows, dust. The terraces are cut in clean steps, and wedge marks in rows show where blocks were split. Timber cranes with counterweights stand on three of the terraces, and a long rail of wooden tracks carries sledges to the loading yard. At the foot of the quarry lie unfinished lintels, columns and an enormous gate-lion with half its mane cut. The quarrymen's barracks have thick walls, and a stone shrine to the stone sits at the second terrace with a basket of red pebbles. Smoke from the cooking fires drifts across the face.

places.name: Dục Nhật Đảo
places.size: A great forested island (on the map about 180 by 260 km): the east shore with the stone arch, one thatched hermit's hut under the trees, the arch about 60 m across, and a few pilgrims' boats; no town.
places.where: Temperate forest at 230 m on an island in the far south-eastern sea, its eastern shore facing open ocean. Water qi. No holder. Nearest: the beast lair Vạn Xà Lâm 182 km. The gate to Phù Tang Cảnh; Mạc Quy Khư, the oldest living person, has lived here since 700. Map crop: a long forested island standing in open ocean, about 180 km wide and 260 km long on the map, brown rocky heights at its southern end, a smaller forested island to the north-west and another to the south-west; the marker is at the north tip, with open ocean to the east.
places.imagined: Sunrise straight out of the water, framed in a ring of sea-worn rock.
places.subject: The place: Dục Nhật Đảo, the Island Where the Sun Bathes, seen from above at sunrise. Setting: a great forested island some hundred and eighty kilometres wide and two hundred and sixty long in a calm blue-violet sea, in the far south-east, with brown rocky heights at its southern end and smaller forested islands off to the north-west and south-west, its eastern shore facing open ocean with no land beyond, a long white line of surf on a crescent of pale sand, a thin mist on the water. The sun, huge and red-gold, is just rising straight out of the water on the horizon, throwing a long bright path across the sea to the shore. On that eastern shore stands a great ring of sea-worn rock, a natural arch about sixty metres across, open to the sunrise, the gate of Phù Tang Cảnh, with the sunlight pouring through its centre and a faint golden shimmer in the air within it as if a second sea lay behind. Dense forest of mulberry and pine covers the island's interior. A single thatched hut sits under the trees above the arch, with a swept yard and a thin thread of smoke, and one tiny old figure sits at its door facing the sun. A handful of pilgrims' small boats lie pulled up on the sand, with figures standing at a respectful distance. Rosy-gold light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. Beyond the arch the first shaft of sun lights the island's whole eastern coast in a band of gold, a pale road across the water to the horizon. Mulberry trees stand in a dark ring above the hut, the oldest of them hung with strips of red silk. A crescent of fine pale sand fronts the arch, with a line of footprints leading to its centre. At the shore a half-ring of eight low stones marks where pilgrims sit, and a cold stream trickles from the hill beside the hut. A single heron stands at the arch's foot.

places.name: Đồ Nam Đảo
places.size: A great hooked island (on the map about 250 km tip to tip): the left arm shown with a vast shallow hollow about 2 km wide in its crown; uninhabited, a few fish offerings in the hollow.
places.where: Grassland at 80 m on an island in the southern sea, coast. Water qi. No holder. Nearest: the hot spring Lãng Ôn Trì 215 km. The great Bằng rests here before flying south; sailors land only to leave fish for a fair wind. Map crop: a huge hook-shaped island of soft green and forested slopes, about 250 km from tip to tip, its arms enclosing a blue bay and ending in a brown volcanic cone at the north-east end; the marker is on the west coast of the left arm.
places.imagined: A wind always blowing south; seabirds wheeling in their thousands over a feather-printed hollow.
places.subject: The place: Đồ Nam Đảo, the Island of the Southward Flight, seen from above a southern sea. Setting: a calm blue sea with long swells, a huge hook-shaped island of soft green and wooded slopes, about two hundred and fifty kilometres from tip to tip, its two long arms enclosing a blue bay and ending in a brown volcanic cone at the north-east end, pale sand beaches and a rim of low rocks, thin cloud streaming south in long strips as if a steady wind blew that way. The crown of the island is pressed into a vast shallow hollow about two kilometres across, oval, as if something enormous had lain there, its bed smooth and shaped with a deeper hollow where a body would lie and two long grooves where wings would spread. The grass in the hollow grows in long swirled streaks like the print of feathers, silver-green and gold, all bending southward. Seabirds wheel over it in their thousands, a cloud of white and grey birds. Nothing is built here. On the shore a single small fishing boat is pulled up on the sand and a few tiny figures walk into the hollow with baskets of fish and lay them in a row at its edge, then stand with faces to the south. Light from the upper left, long soft shadows, the whole scene calm and immense. A single white line of surf marks the island's western shore, and shoals of pale sand show as lighter bands in the blue. On the near arm the green grass at the hollow's rim runs in long combed lines southward, and a few stunted trees lean in the same direction. Fish offerings lie in a neat row at the hollow's southern lip, each wrapped in a leaf. Some sailors' cairns of white coral stone stand on the beach. Far off, white wings lift in a wave from the hollow, then settle.

places.name: Xích Thành Môn
places.size: A destroyed great sect's gate cut into sea cliffs: a ruined domain about 3 km along the coast, once about 150 buildings and 1,200 people, now fire-blackened terraces open to the sky; no one lives there.
places.where: Steppe at 150 m on the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu, among red cliffs and vents. Water qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung; a former sect, founded 250 by Tôn Hà Khởi, destroyed under the Compact's first writ. Nearest: the village Tân Sinh 195 km, the spirit vein Tàn Hỏa Mạch 236 km. Map crop: the east coast of a mainland of golden-brown hills with forest strips and bare grey rock, the sea to the east; the cliffs stand at the shore.
places.imagined: Dusk: red cliffs like banks of rosy cloud, gutted halls, fresh pale quarry scars.
places.subject: The place: Xích Thành Môn, the Red Cliff Gate, a destroyed sect, seen from above the coast of a red land at dusk. Setting: cliffs of deep red rock rising in rounded tiers like banks of rosy cloud above a calm violet sea, dry steppe grass on top, thin smoke from vents rising in the distance, and a pink sky. Into the cliffs are cut the broken terraces and gutted halls of the old gate along about three kilometres of coast: tiers of terraces cut into the red rock, linked by broken stairs and galleries, the halls roofless and their fire-blackened walls open to the sky, fallen towers, an arched sea gate half collapsed with the harbour wall stumps in the water, a tall burned banner-mast snapped in two, and hundreds of burned-out buildings as black outlines on the terraces, windows empty, ash-grey rubble. Fresh pale quarry scars show where stone has lately been taken away to rebuild elsewhere, bright cut faces against the old soot, with a path of sledge tracks leading off. Nobody grazes here; the grass is untouched. A faint heat shimmer rises from a vent crack on one terrace, and the cliffs glow warm. A few tiny figures on the path stop at a distance. Light from the upper left, long red shadows. Around the ruin, vent cracks release thin steam in a dozen places, and the red earth is hot to the touch in the evening. The great hall's roof beams lie in a black heap, and a stair of two hundred steps still climbs the top terrace. The arched sea-gate is thirty metres across, with the stumps of two lighthouse towers on either side, and the pale quarry scars are laid in clean square steps. At the broken banner-mast's foot lies a mass of fire-silk ash, and a few red threads still flutter from a split in its post. The headland beyond the gate is bare and swept by wind.

places.name: Thôn Hải Môn
places.size: A pirates' ruined hold on the southern tip of a long hooked forested island (on the map about 180 km long): a sea cave large enough for a ship, about 30 burned shells and a broken quay; no people but treasure seekers.
places.where: Temperate forest at 30 m on an islet of the southern gulf ringed by rocks, coast. Water qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung; a former sect, the pirates' hold founded 640 by Ô Kình Hải, ended 781. Nearest: the village Phá Lãng 125 km, the forest Thanh Da Lâm 146 km. Map crop: a long hooked narrow forested island standing alone in a green-blue southern sea, about 180 km from end to end on the map, at the world's southern edge (the map is cut off below); the hold lies at the island's southern tip.
places.imagined: Low tide at dawn, a black sea-cave mouth with a broken log boom and heaped charred timbers inside.
places.subject: The place: Thôn Hải Môn, the Gate That Swallows the Sea, a pirates' ruined hold, seen from above a gulf at low tide. Setting: a hooked, narrow forested island about a hundred and eighty kilometres from end to end, standing alone in a green-blue southern sea at the world's southern edge, with the old hold on its southern tip, ringed by black rocks and white surf, tangled dark forest on its top, a few stunted pines, and a bare crown. At the waterline of the sheltered side gapes the black mouth of a great sea cave, wide and tall enough to take a ship, its rim scorched black, with the stumps of a broken log boom still standing across the mouth in two lines of black posts, and charred timbers of the old hold lying in heaps inside the entrance, with the hulk of a burned ship wedged against the rocks. On the islet's slopes, about thirty burned-out shells of stone and timber buildings, a collapsed lookout tower and a long broken quay and slipway, with scorched ground and ash-grey pockets where the forest has not come back. Wet trenches of holes dug in the ash by treasure seekers, and a small boat pulled up on the shingle with two tiny figures digging and a third waiting, away from the cave. Pale dawn light from the upper left, long shadows, mist on the water. Black rocks ring the tip, and white surf breaks on them in a continuous line. The cave's roof is high enough for masts, and the water within is dark green. On the slope above stand a toppled watchtower and the stubs of a palisade; its logs lie as charcoal in a long line. A ship's ribs lie on the strand, grown with weed. The treasure seekers' trenches, a score of them, pit the ash in rows like graves. A line of scorched anchors, six of them, lies on the beach where the fleet once rode.

places.name: Vạn Xà Lâm
places.size: A deep jungle lair covering a long island (about 140 km on the map); no buildings, only a collectors' camp of two or three tents on the shore in the dry season.
places.where: Jungle at 260 m, inland, at the far end of Đan Huyệt Châu, the farthest lair from any town. Water qi. No holder; resource beast bone. Nearest: the island Dục Nhật 182 km, the forest Thanh Da Lâm 304 km. Map crop: a dark jungle island about 140 km long standing in a blue sea, brown rocky heights at its southern end, a second island with a volcanic cone to the west; the marker is on the island's west coast.
places.imagined: Humid stillness; strangler figs wrapped over a black pool, snakes sunning on grey roots.
places.subject: The place: Vạn Xà Lâm, the Forest of Ten Thousand Snakes, seen from above a deep jungle. Setting: a dark jungle island about a hundred and forty kilometres long, its steaming green canopy rolling in low hills down to rocky brown heights at the south end, a second volcanic island visible to the west across the blue sea, mist rising in the hollows, a hot hazy sky. Giant strangler figs, dozens of them, have wrapped and swallowed older trees: huge tangled columns of grey roots, braided and knotted, rising above the canopy like the towers of a ruined city. In a clearing among them lies a black, still pool about two hundred metres across, under grey roots that coil over it and down into the water like nests of snakes, and real snakes lie sunning on them, hundreds of them, of every kind and colour: green, banded black and yellow, bright red, and a few of enormous size, as thick as a man and as long as a house, draped over high roots. Egrets and eagles hang over. A deep green silence. At the far edge of the jungle, a collectors' camp of three small tents with a smoking fire and drying racks for shed skins, and two tiny figures in thick leather leggings moving carefully with long forked poles and jars. Steamy gold light from the upper left shafting through the leaves. The pool is ringed by a collar of pale roots and black mud, and the snakes' bodies shine in the shafts of light like coils of wet rope. Some branches sag beneath a dozen sleeping snakes. The fig roots form buttresses large enough to hide a house, with hollows lined with shed skins like drifts of paper. On the strand a narrow shingle beach rises to a line of tall trees, and the collectors' tents hold racks of glass jars, forked poles and thick leather gloves. A single enormous snake, an elder, rests across a root bridge.

places.name: Chu Sa Tuyền
places.size: A single round hot spring about 40 m across in a jungle clearing, an overflow stream about 2 km long; a bath shelter or two.
places.where: Jungle at 30 m, inland, in Đan Huyệt Châu. Water qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Resource: spirit spring water. Nearest: the lava vent Luyện Vũ Huyệt 90 km, the ruin Lưu Hỏa Các 257 km. Map crop: the south bend of a long U-shaped jungle island with a smoking volcanic cone on its north-east arm and open blue sea around; the spring is near the island's south coast.
places.imagined: A round spring boiling up blood-red, vermilion stream through pale steaming jungle.
places.subject: The place: Chu Sa Tuyền, the Cinnabar Spring, seen from above a jungle clearing. Setting: dense jungle in dark green on the south bend of a long U-shaped island with a smoking volcanic cone rising on its north-east arm and blue sea around, pale steam rising among the trees until the whole forest looks washed pale and misty, a hot damp sky. In a clearing, a single round hot spring about forty metres across boils up blood-red from the ground, steaming hard, its surface roiling in slow bubbles and rings, with a crust of bright orange-red mineral around its rim and white steam clouds lifting. Its overflow runs away through the trees in a bright vermilion stream about ten metres wide and two kilometres long, winding in loops through the jungle, staining the rocks and banks red and orange, with pink-white mineral shelves where it falls over small ledges. Around the spring, a flat rock terrace and a few simple bathing platforms of timber with thatched shelters, two of them, with stone steps down into the water. A few fire cultivators in pink-stained skin and wet robes soak in the water, tiny figures in red-dyed robes, while a herbalist scrapes red crust from the stream bed with a flat knife and a basket. Hot gold light from the upper left through steam, long shadows. The mineral crust around the spring is in rings of orange, rose and white, as thick as a hand, and the stream carries a bright red slurry that settles in the pools along its length. Bamboo pipes bring a little of the hot water to the bathing platforms. The stream's banks are stained rust up to the height of a hand, and the trees along it have red-tinged leaf-bases. A rack of clay pots stands by the herbalist's path, each filled with scraped crust, and a woven screen shades the platform from the sun.

places.name: Chúc Dung Khẩu
places.size: A volcanic cone about 3 km across with a crater about 600 m wide shaped like an open mouth; a watch post of Phượng Minh Cung with about 20 watchers, a few huts.
places.where: Volcano at 550 m on the east coast of Đan Huyệt Châu. Fire qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Resource: earth-fire essence. Named for the fire god Chúc Dung; the most dangerous place in the vermilion caves. Nearest: the ruin Hỏa Ti Trấn 75 km, the village Tang Âm 152 km. Map crop: a great grey-brown volcanic cone about 100 km across at its base on a narrow neck of land between a gulf on the west and open sea on the east, red-gold grass and dark forest on its lower slopes; the marker is on the cone's south-east slope.
places.imagined: A thin tongue of lava creeping down a notch in the lip, hissing where it meets wet rock.
places.subject: The place: Chúc Dung Khẩu, the Mouth of the Fire God, seen from above on the east coast of a red land. Setting: a great grey-brown volcanic cone, a hundred kilometres across at its base, rising on a narrow neck of land between a blue gulf on the west and the open sea on the east, red-gold grass and dark forest on its lower slopes, steam and smoke rising in a thick column, and a hazy orange sky. The cone opens in a wide crater about six hundred metres across whose lip is shaped like an open mouth: a lower jagged lip and a higher overhanging upper lip with black rock like teeth. Inside, lava glows bright orange in a roiling lake, with white-hot cracks, and a thin tongue of it creeps down a notch in the rim, hissing and steaming where it meets wet rock, a glowing red line about two hundred metres long over black. Black ash lies in streaks down the cone, and a fan of old cooled lava runs toward the sea. On a safer ridge about a kilometre off stands a watch post of Phượng Minh Cung: a stone tower with a signal fire basin, three huts, and a flagpole bare of cloth, about twenty watchers, tiny figures in red-brown, and a fishing boat offshore. Glow of lava under the smoke, hot gold light from the upper left, long shadows. Ash drifts in long pale fans downhill, and the rim's upper lip shows rust-coloured cracks and glowing crevices. At the watch post a line of nine stone cairns marks the safe path, and the signal fire-basin holds a stack of brushwood and pitch. A pair of fishing boats works the east coast, and their crews glance at the plume. Along the shore, heaps of pumice float in the surf in drifts of grey stones. A sacrificial stone stands on a ledge near the lip, bare of any offering.

places.name: Hỏa Ti Trấn
places.size: A great sect's present seat, moved here in 1162, an old fire-silk town grown into a palace-domain: about 4 km across, about 300 members plus servants and mortal families (about 3,000 residents), about 300 buildings.
places.where: High mountain biome at 280 m, inland, in the vent country of Đan Huyệt Châu. Fire qi. Holder Phần Vũ Đường by the tag, but the great sect Phượng Minh Cung's court since 1162, its inner gate cultivating here since 592. Nearest: the lava vent Chúc Dung Khẩu 75 km, Phần Vũ Đường 125 km. Map crop: a great volcanic cone of grey-white crater rim and dark interior on a neck of green land between a gulf on the west and the open sea on the east, dark forest on its east flank and rolling grass to the north; the marker is on the north rim. Per the sect pages it is the great sect's present seat (moved 1162), though the map marks it as a ruin.
places.imagined: Evening: a red palace-town with skeins of crimson fire-silk drying in long banners, vent smoke rising behind.
places.subject: The place: Hỏa Ti Trấn, the Fire-Silk Town, now the court of the great sect of the Phoenix, seen from above at evening. Setting: a neck of green and golden land between a blue gulf on the west and the open sea on the east, with rolling grass and dark forest to the north and east; in its middle rises a great volcanic cone with a pale grey-white crater rim and a dark ashen bowl inside, and the sect's domain lies along the cone's northern rim and slopes, about four kilometres across. Around the rim stand about three hundred buildings: red-lacquered halls with golden-brown glazed roofs rising in stepped terraces, covered galleries linking them, gate towers on four walls, a great audience hall on the rim's highest point, and a ring wall of red-brown stone. Within it the old fire-silk quarter still crowds the northern slope: narrow lanes, dye-houses, reeling halls with tall chimneys, and weavers' houses of grey tile. Everywhere hang skeins and banners of crimson, orange and gold fire-silk on long poles and frames, hundreds of metres of fluttering cloth in rows like flames, so the whole rim glows. A young wutong grove has been planted along the ridge to the north in tidy rows, with a fine young tree standing alone on the highest court to recall the old seat. From the dark crater a thin plume of vent smoke leans east on the sea wind, and the walls glow faintly with its heat. Down the slope a pale road runs to a market gate where silk caravans and ox-carts queue. About three thousand people, servants, weavers, mortal families and cultivators, move in the streets and courts as tiny figures. Hot gold evening light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right.

places.name: Lưu Hỏa Các
places.size: A ruined sect pavilion on a coast: a compound about 400 m across, once about 40 buildings, now burned shells and a collapsed pavilion; no residents.
places.where: Jungle at 460 m, on the coast, no river. Water qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung; a former sect. Nearest: the lava vent Luyện Vũ Huyệt 168 km, the hot spring Chu Sa Tuyền 257 km. Map crop: the north headland of a long hooked jungle island, a grey rocky volcanic peak to the south-west, small islets offshore, and open blue sea all round; the ruin faces a small rocky cove.
places.imagined: Dusk: jungle swallowing a once-fine pavilion above a quiet sea.
places.subject: The place: Lưu Hỏa Các, the Pavilion of Flowing Fire, a ruined sect seat, seen from above a jungle coast at dusk. Setting: green jungle on steep hills at the north tip of a long hooked jungle island, a grey rocky peak rising to the south-west, small islets offshore, all tumbling down to a blue-green sea, a small rocky cove with a pale beach below, a few offshore stacks, low cloud with a red-gold sunset. On a ridge above the cove stand the ruins of a sect compound about four hundred metres across, within a broken whitewashed wall, once about forty buildings: a collapsed main pavilion whose red-lacquered pillars still stand in a ring around a fallen roof, scorched halls with blackened beams open to the sky, burned dormitories, a long gallery with half its columns, a courtyard of cracked paving with a dry fountain basin, and a stair of white stone running down toward the cove, half buried in leaves. Creepers and strangler figs have swallowed the walls and roofs, with orange flowers hanging from the broken eaves, and a shimmer of black soot stains the stones. A fisher's path leads up from the beach, and two tiny figures stand at the foot of the stair, peering up, with a small boat on the sand. Light from the upper left, warm and fading, long shadows to the lower right. The pavilion's red pillars number sixteen, each wrapped in a spiral of creeper; the roof lies in the middle in a mass of green-glazed tile. The stair of white stone has two hundred and forty steps, with lion-headed newel posts, and in the dusk the white of the stone is almost the only clean thing. A bell hangs cracked in the tower frame. The fisher's boat is of six mended planks, and the fishers pay a coin on the lowest step. At the cove's far end a small flock of sea-birds nests in the burned gatehouse.

places.name: Chức Hà Các
places.size: A minor sect of weavers, reelers and leaf-pickers: about 40 people, a walled compound about 300 m across with about 35 buildings and mulberry rows, founded 1150.
places.where: Grassland at 40 m on the coast of Đan Huyệt Châu. Water qi. Righteous vassal of Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the village Trúc Lâu 135 km, the spirit vein Thanh Can Mạch 230 km. Map crop: the west coast of a long north-south grass-and-forest landmass about 360 km wide, a blue gulf on the west and the sea on the east; the sect sits on the western shore.
places.imagined: Morning, long bolts of cloud-coloured silk hung out to dry across the whole compound, like a sunrise on cloth.
places.subject: The place: Chức Hà Các, the Pavilion of Weaving Sunrise Cloud, a small sect of weavers, seen from above coastal grassland. Setting: flat pale grassland by a calm blue sea, a low pale shore, fields of mulberry in long dark-green rows, and a distant smoking vent far inland. The compound is a walled yard about three hundred metres across with a whitewashed wall and one gate, about thirty-five buildings: a long weaving hall with a row of wide windows and a tiered roof, a reeling house with a tall chimney and steaming vats, an airy dye-house, dormitories, a leaf-store, a shed of looms, and a small shrine to the weaving goddess. Over the whole yard stand twelve long poles each hung with sixteen bolts of silk in sunrise colours, pink, apricot, gold, rose, pale violet, each twelve metres long, about two hundred bolts fluttering in the sea wind like a cloud lit by dawn. Around the compound lie mulberry rows, with leaf-pickers in headscarves moving along them with baskets, and about forty weavers, reelers and pickers, tiny figures, at work. Soft pink-gold light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. The shadows of the cloth cross the yard as pink and gold bars. The looms are in a shed of forty frames, and the weavers work in rows, with a clack that carries to the sea. The reeling house holds twelve vats, and a woman lifts thread in a shining skein. A small shrine to the weaving goddess has a basket of cocoons at its foot. The mulberry rows end at a low wall with a gate and a lane of crushed shell to the shore, where a boat unloads bales of raw silk.
